analysisDescription: Using the paper "A Living Framework for Understanding Cooperative Games" as support, I analyzed Phasmophobia while playing it solo and while observing past recorded playthroughs where I played with a group.
frameworkComments: The framework was relatively easy to use and understand but it felt like it was missing some options in the last two topics (Asymmetry and Relations between Player Actions)

dimensionExamples.example: A player must first create a private or public room/lobby (or join one). Other players can then access the room by a code if private creating a party, or simply by searching the room list if public. Meaning you create a party by sending a code to the desired people.

dimension.title: Party Creation
dimension.description: Party Creation encompasses all games where groups are defined by the players themselves prior to initiating gameplay, typically leveraging friend lists or co-located party creation.

dimensionExamples.example: To look for a group, a player can access the server browser where the public lobbies are.

dimension.title: Looking for Group
dimension.description: Looking for Group happens when there are grouping mechanisms that allow players to formally look for and create a group/party. This is typically achieved through matchmaking or looking for group queues.

dimensionExamples.example: The goal consists on Players finding where and what type is the ghost exactly. There is also mini objectives that all players in the current lobby share.

dimension.title: Shared
dimension.description: Shared goals consist of singular objectives that multiple players pursue and work together to achieve

dimensionExamples.example: Players progress individually by earning money and experience points. There is also a hint of party progression since players that die in-game can still reap rewards if the last remaining player survives and allows for more objectives and goals completed, and players can benefit from equipment and money of other players.

dimension.title: Individual
dimension.description: Individual progression is defined by individual choice and the individual impact of the progression. In-game activities can vary from individual to fully cooperative but progression affects the individual.

dimensionExamples.example: Each player controls a human character

dimension.title: Single
dimension.description: Single applies to any game where players have control of one single entity.

dimensionExamples.example: There is a set of pre-made character models that can be chosen by players. Does not affect gameplay (only affects height of line of sight slightly).

dimension.title: Arbitrary
dimension.description: Arbitrary means that all player entities are equal in their ability to act upon the world. If a selection exists, it is merely an aesthetic choice.

dimensionExamples.example: No change is present.

dimension.title: Static
dimension.description: When the player's entity is constant throughout gameplay.

dimensionExamples.example: No relationships are present.

dimension.title: Individuals
dimension.description: Individuals describes when players’ entities have no established relationship with each other, which affects gameplay.

dimensionExamples.example: Players that die enter a 'limbo' world where they can interact with some objects, phase through doors and cannot be hunted by the ghost. The players who are still alive cant see them which offers 2 unique perspectives on the same map/world.

dimension.title: Unique
dimension.description: Unique world views correspond to the players having access to the same world but having unique perspectives on it (e.g. the different fog of war across teammates is a simple instance of a unique world view).

dimensionExamples.example: Players control viewpoints through separate screens

dimension.title: Distinct
dimension.description: Distinct refers to when each player has control of their own individual viewpoint, typically through separate screens.

dimensionExamples.example: Players are accomplishing the same tasks together but they can decide between themselves who does what, and what tasks/objectives are worth doing. In the end they can always still retreat (end a game session) without doing any major objectives.

dimension.title: Free Collaboration
dimension.description: In free collaboration, players can take on available tasks as they wish and decide how to contribute.

dimensionExamples.example: Players are playing simultaneously.

dimension.title: Concurrent Collaboration
dimension.description: In concurrent collaboration, players have to perform gameplay tasks concurrently.

dimensionExamples.example: Players are incentivized to talk to each other to delegate tasks, convey what clues they already possess, to debate what is the ghost type, to alert for hunts etc.. Furthermore, they also need to communicate with the ghost itself making this communication a requirement in certain types of investigations.

dimension.title: Required/Incentivised
dimension.description: When Required/Incentivised, the game challenges require players to communicate (e.g. when there is essential asymmetric information), or incentivised through challenges that are made easier through it (e.g. coordinating combined actions for maximum effect).

dimensionExamples.example: Players can only communicate in-game through voice chat in proximity mode or in radio/global mode. Dead players can also sometimes convey simple communication through throwing objects but this is rather lackluster.

dimension.title: Voice Chat
dimension.description: Support for players to communicate using their voice

dimensionExamples.example: Players rely on others to lighten up the challenging maps and investigations. Although playing alone is not impossible nor very difficult, playing with a group allows for a bigger money poll, more resources/equipment,  more lives (it is game over when all players in a map are dead) and more fun overall.

dimension.title: Fixed Difficulty
dimension.description: Fixed Difficulty, when games purposefully do not adapt the difficulty to player count, making some challenges near impossible without more players collaborating. While some players can take it as a challenge to complete on their own, others can rely on their fellow players to lighten up the challenge.

dimensionExamples.example: Since all players share the same goal and objective, almost all actions that a player takes in finding/discovering the ghost assist all other players. Assistive actions are also present after the game starts (i.e.: a player can add his high tier equipment to the van after the game starts, helping players who don't have access to that higher tier yet.)

dimension.title: Assistive Actions
dimension.description: Assistive Actions encompass actions that one player performs to the benefit of other/s (i.e. note that the player can have indirect benefits such as reviving others to increase their own chances of success). In these games, players can support and assist other players in achieving their objectives.

dimensionExamples.example: There can also be piggy-backing: a player that for example has fear of entering the house or is simply AFK for the majority of the session can reap the benefits of the other player that completed the objectives and discovered the ghost. In the end both receive the same amount of money and experience points if the carrying player shares the correct ghost type.

dimension.title: Piggy-Backing
dimension.description: Piggy-Backing refers to a specific mechanic, where one player's performance can be leveraged for others to bypass challenges.

dimensionExamples.example: Sanity, sanity 'pills', smudge sticks and crucifixes

dimension.title: Consumables
dimension.description: Consumables refer to items that exist in a limited amount and can be utilised by players to invoke an effect (usually existing as a form of currency, materials, or food) or are not consumed on purpose by players but support the gameplay (e.g., health, energy). Consumables are shared when the agency to consume and manage them pertains to more than one player.

dimensionExamples.example: Players can unlock new tiers of equipment by leveling up. These new tiers often provide better utility than the old ones. Players can share high tier equipment with others in-game.

dimension.title: Unlockables
dimension.description: Unlockables refer to content available in the gameplay but not accessible up until players are able and choose to get access to it. Usually, games limit the number of unlocks a player can acquire. Unlockables are shared when the decision to unlock new content pertains to more than one player. The effect of the unlockables may or may not be shared (it might affect only one player, but they would still be shared if more than one player could make the decision).

dimensionExamples.example: There are cursed objects within a map that players can interact with. There is also the main interactable challenge of the game: the ghost, where players can interact with him by using cursed objects, using certain equipment and talking through voice chat.

dimension.title: Interactables
dimension.description: Interactables refer to virtual objects and non-player characters/entities within the environment that respond to players’ actions. Interactables can be moved, shaped, or activated (e.g., a cannon that shoots when the player interacts with it). In some cases, interactables are also consumable (e.g., food in Overcooked is transported and modified as an interactable, but also consumed to complete the recipes). Interactables are shared when their state and attributes can be affected by more than one player.

dimensionExamples.example: There is usually no relevant asymmetry in Phasmophobia, but sometimes there can be information asymmetry where a dead player can locate the exact location of the ghost by spectating it during a hunt, or when a player discovered a clue/evidence essential to the main goal while others don't  know of it yet. Information is usually shared by the own will of the players to unsure that if only one survives, it can still access all info gathered and reach a conclusion that benefits everyone.

dimension.title: Information
dimension.description: Information, as described by Harris et al. 2016, is where one player knows something other players do not. In cooperative games, this is leveraged by ensuring the information is needed to be shared, or acted upon by more than the player with access to the knowledge. This is typically instantiated with players having Distinct - Player Views and Worlds.

dimensionExamples.example: There are no real asymmetric weaknesses/strengths in this game but players can complement each other by coordinating on certain actions. ( If player A wants to take a photo of the ghost, another player can complement and coordinate with player A by using a smudge stick that repels ghost attacks while player A uses the camera, allowing both to escape death.)

dimension.title: Complementarity
dimension.description: Complementarity, extended from Rocha et. al rocha2008game, corresponds to when player actions are designed to balance each other’s weaknesses or so that strengths complement each other. It is typically achieved through asymmetric game design, with each player bringing something to the shared experience.
